what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Ask politely for usage, a pause and a refund
sections.para: A helper-run, agent-driven service for unused subscriptions: ask the company for a usage record while doing our own analysis, then request a suspend mode and a refund, and stop paying either way. Results go into an open Creative Commons register. The helper earns 10% of three months' savings and 20% of recoveries.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Ask, pause, refund, stop paying, and publish the results
sections.para: Unwanted UK subscriptions cost £1.6 billion a year. The service asks for usage, then politely for a pause and refund, and stops payments regardless; refunds are mostly goodwill, with access requests only for data. Claude in Chrome and the Gmail connector do the work; the freelancer types secrets and sends drafts.

sections.label: The subscriptions we keep
sections.line: People keep paying for subscriptions they barely use
sections.para: Subscriptions linger because they hold data and restarting is painful. The UK government estimates 155 million active subscriptions, with £1.6 billion a year spent on unwanted ones, and Citizens Advice found £688 million spent on unused ones. A subscription is a discount for regular use, not rent on something you may ignore.

sections.label: Step one: ask them what we used, and work it out ourselves
sections.line: Start by asking for usage and analysing it ourselves
sections.para: The first move is a polite email asking for a monthly breakdown of logins, storage and seats, which concedes nothing. In parallel, statements, invoices and the account's dashboards are exported into the person's own vault and analysed by an agent. Where the two sets of numbers disagree, that becomes the next question.

sections.label: Step two: a friendly request for a pause and a refund
sections.line: A warm letter asks for a pause and refund
sections.para: Days later, with evidence in hand, the letter sets out what was paid, when it was last used and what the product was worth, and praises it honestly. It asks for a pause that keeps the data and a refund for unused months. Netflix, Zoom, YouTube Premium, Audible and Hulu already offer pauses.

sections.label: Stop the bleeding
sections.line: Stop the payments whatever the refund answer, exporting first
sections.para: Whether or not money comes back, the payments stop: pause if possible, otherwise export the data and cancel. Exporting first matters because the data is why the account was kept. Watch early-exit terms, such as Adobe's US fee of half the remaining balance on annual plans paid monthly.

sections.label: What the law does, and what it does not
sections.line: Unused months are rarely refundable, but rules favour customers
sections.para: Refunds are owed only in narrow cases such as cooling-off periods or missing cancellation information, so most will be goodwill. The UK's DMCC Act subscription rules arrive in January 2027, the EU withdrawal button applied from 19 June 2026, and California's AB 2863 since July 2025, while the FTC restarts its rule.

sections.label: If nobody answers: the right of access
sections.line: Access requests are for data, never a refund lever
sections.para: If the first letter gets no reply, a UK GDPR access request follows: a one-month response, usually free, and the EDPB includes activity logs in scope. A helper with authority can make it. The request must be genuine and never bundled with a demand, so the refund conversation stays separate.

sections.label: An open register, under Creative Commons
sections.line: An open register records which companies refund, without adjectives
sections.para: The whole method is published under Creative Commons, with contacts, templates, pause options, response times and outcomes for each company. Following the subscriptions site's rules: records not verdicts, silence as a row, no first refusals published, and the good path as prominent as the bad. It publishes company behaviour, never a person's case.

sections.label: A service for helpers
sections.line: Low fees mean the agents must do the work
sections.para: Anyone organised could be the helper, paid 10% of three months' savings and 20% of recoveries, against Rocket Money's 35% to 60%. On the average £14 unwanted subscription that is £4.20 for stopping it and £16.80 for recovering six months, so it only pays across many subscriptions with agents doing the work.

sections.label: Done by agents, under a policy
sections.line: The freelancer types secrets; agents do the rest
sections.para: Claude in Chrome drives the browser, pausing at logins for the freelancer, and the Gmail connector writes drafts the freelancer sends. Vaults with Issues-FS and Email-FS are the interface. Drafts-only is a policy, not a tool limit, since a signed-in session has the account's whole reach, and Anthropic advises against financial-account use.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: An untested MVP with goodwill refunds and open risks
sections.para: Not yet run beyond a March statement pipeline; beta users will try it on their own subscriptions. Refunds are mostly goodwill, consumer rules may not cover businesses, the law is as at 13 October 2026, and the register is empty. The signed-in session's reach and how access is shared remain open questions.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: government figures, consumer law and Anthropic's tooling docs
sections.para: Drafted from two voice memos of 13 October 2026, with rules from subscriptions.sgit.ai. Sources include the UK government's 9 August 2026 announcement, Citizens Advice, the DMCC Act, the Consumer Contracts Regulations, ICO and EDPB guidance, Netflix, Zoom and Adobe help pages, Rocket Money, and Anthropic's Claude in Chrome documentation.
